summary: Follow-up postmortem with Orion Health after a 2-hour service disruption tied to KV cache eviction and autoscaler misconfiguration. Team reviewed root cause, immediate mitigations, longer-term reliability changes and security questions; agreed on benchmarks and a canary rollout plan.
topics: Root cause: KV cache / long-context OOMs
Mitigations: fallback routing, retry/backoff, seq-length caps
Security questions: KMS, audit logs, VPC peering
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-30 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~50 minutes | Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Redwood CSM), Sarah Lin (Orion SRE), Rajesh Kumar (Orion Eng Mgr), Alex Park (Orion CTO)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. This is Maya from Redwood, I'll kick us off — we wanted to walk through the postmortem, confirm the root cause, and align on fixes and next steps.
[00:14] Sarah: Thanks, yeah appreciate you guys doing this. We had a pretty bad hit Wednesday afternoon. Roughly two hours of elevated errors, latency spike then partial outages for our chat flows.
[00:28] Liam: Right, and we rebuilt the timeline in the doc we shared — link in chat, postmortem.pdf. Short version: increase in long-context requests caused sustained KV cache pressure which triggered evictions; that combined with a threshold in the autoscaler that didn't burst fast enough, so nodes started OOM-ing and requests were getting 5xx or hanging.
[00:47] Rajesh: To be clear, when you say KV cache evictions, is that the per-model kv-store or something at the runtime level? We saw a lot of token re-generation and repeated full-context reloads.
[01:03] Liam: Good question. It's the runtime-level KV cache for decoder key/values. In our tracing, the large sequences forced many cache entries and some long-lived sessions had larger than expected KV usage. When entries were evicted, subsequent requests had to repopulate, which increased latency and memory spikes. The eviction pattern caused thrashing.
[01:23] Alex: Was this an issue with our workload pattern or with the model variant you had in the dedicated pool?
[01:30] Maya: It's both — your workload had more >8k token sessions than we'd anticipated from the initial sizing. Also, there was an autoscaler policy on your dedicated pool with a conservative scale-up step size and cooldown window; combined those two factors meant the system couldn't catch up quickly when memory pressure spiked.
[01:48] Sarah: We saw a ton of partial retries, and some of our clients retried aggressively which made it worse. We probably need guidance on retry/backoff best practices since some of our SDK retries are pretty aggressive.
[02:05] Priya: We'll add recommended retry patterns to the follow-up docs. Generally exponential backoff with jitter, and cap retries at 3 for streaming endpoints.
[02:17] [02:20] Liam: Also pulled logs — there's a sequence of ~12 requests from the same session that had 16k tokens each; we didn't have sequence caps on the ingress side, so the runtime got overloaded.
[02:32] Sarah: Hm, those were from a single integration. We'll identify the app ID and either patch client or put a per-session cap.
[02:41] Rajesh: On the autoscaler, what change do you recommend? Increase target utilization or change the step size?
[02:50] Liam: Two-pronged: lower the memory headroom target so scale-up occurs earlier (e.g., trigger at 65% instead of 80%), and increase the max step count so you can add more nodes in one event. Also shorten the cooldown so the system can react to sustained spikes.
[03:08] Alex: Any risk of over-scaling and driving cost?
[03:11] Maya: There's a tradeoff — we'll model burst-only capacity vs committed capacity. For immediate reliability, we recommend a small burst pool you pay for only when used, plus the autoscaler changes. We'll send expected cost delta in the pricing addendum.
[03:27] Sarah: Security / compliance people also asked about the logs and KMS usage during the incident — were any keys rotated or was any data exfiltrated?
[03:36] Liam: No evidence of data exfiltration. Keys were stable; we did see increased audit log volume which we'll share. For KMS, your setup uses customer-managed keys; we can confirm logs in the KMS dashboard. We'll include KMS integration docs and the network diagram.
[03:55] Rajesh: Great. Also, can we discuss fallback routing? For a short window during the incident you silently downgraded a subset of traffic to a smaller model, is that correct?
[04:05] Maya: Yes, we had an automated fallback to a smaller model variant to keep latency SLOs; that was part of the graceful degradation plan. We flagged it in the incident — some responses had slightly degraded semantics which your team noticed.
[04:20] Sarah: That caused a few downstream regressions in our checks. We need an explicit canary so we can validate output quality before routing live traffic.
[04:28] Priya: Agreed — the canary rollout plan is in the doc. We'll run a 2-hour canary on a dedicated pool with mirrored traffic and your eval prompts.
[04:40] [05:00] Liam: On longer-term fixes: 1) ingress-side seq-length caps and request validation, 2) runtime memory guardrails and smarter eviction heuristics (we have a tuning patch prepared), 3) autoscaler policy updates, 4) improved tracing for KV cache churn.
[05:18] Rajesh: Can you explain the "smarter eviction heuristics"?
[05:21] Liam: Right — instead of pure recency-based eviction, we'll add weights for session affinity and predicted re-use. Short-lived sessions with one-shot requests are lower priority to keep; long-running dialogues that frequently reuse KV will be retained. This reduces repopulation cost.
[05:38] Sarah: Any timeline on that kernel/release?
[05:41] Liam: We can ship a tuning patch to runtime next week (target 2026-04-06) and a more robust heuristic in 2-3 sprints. The immediate patch reduces max KV memory per session and adds guardrails.
[05:53] Alex: For our compliance team, can you annotate what happened in the audit logs and provide the window with affected request IDs? We'll need that for the internal postmortem.
[06:04] Maya: Yes we'll include a CSV of affected request IDs and timestamps. Liam, can you attach the traces?
[06:09] Liam: Yep. I'll include the traces and a light playbook.
[06:12] Sarah: About retries, our SDK is currently set to 5 retries for streaming. We'll drop to 3 and add jitter.
[06:20] [06:45] Priya: Quick note — security wants to do a KMS review and verify HSM-backed keys if possible, also SSO/SAML audit for people who had access to the dedicated pool.
[06:32] Maya: We'll schedule an SSO review with your security folks. I'll put that on the next steps.
[06:40] Rajesh: Are there configuration flags we can tune from Orion side to avoid this class of incidents?
[06:46] Liam: Yes — request validation, session caps, less aggressive client retries, and tagging heavy sessions so they go to a separate capacity pool. We can help you set up a "long-running sessions" pool with different QPS caps.
[07:01] Sarah: We're also worried about billing surprises. When you burst more, how will that show up on our monthly invoice?
[07:09] Maya: We'll provide an example cost model in the addendum showing delta between base reserved capacity and burst usage for the incident window. You can set hard budget limits or alerts to prevent unbounded spend.
[07:22] [07:30] Liam: One more technical note: we observed a bug in the KV eviction counter where two concurrent eviction signals could double-count and accelerate the evictions — that's a separate bug fix we'll include in the patch.
[07:42] Rajesh: Fix priority?
[07:44] Liam: High for the counter bug — we'll patch within 48 hours as it's a correctness issue. The heuristic change is medium priority and will be in the next release cycle.
[07:56] Alex: Ok so to recap: patch for KV counter within 48 hours, runtime tuning patch next week, autoscaler config changes, canary test with Orion evals, security/KMS review, and send final postmortem doc.
[08:14] Maya: That's right. Any other outstanding asks?
[08:18] Sarah: Please add the exact list of affected request IDs and provide the playbook steps we should run if we see similar symptoms.
[08:26] Priya: We'll include a runbook snippet and alert thresholds.
[08:30] [08:45] Liam: I'll also add recommended Prometheus/Grafana thresholds — memory per node, KV eviction rate, request queue depth.
[08:55] Maya: Great. We'll aim to share the consolidated postmortem and the pricing addendum by Friday.
[09:05] Rajesh: Thanks everyone. Appreciate the quick turnaround.
[09:12] Alex: Thanks.
[09:15] Maya: Thanks all, we'll follow up in the ticket with attachments and set the bench run.

Meeting end. Attachments referenced: postmortem.pdf, kv-traces.csv, autoscaler-policy.yaml, security-kms-integration.pdf, canary-plan.docx, pricing_addendum.xlsx
